title: MB0-02108
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, a 25-year-old citizen of Mexico, is claiming refugee protection in Canada under section 96 and paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

XXXXXXXXX alleges that his father had been imprisoned for tax evasion and was released after taking legal action. After his release, he received letters in which he was asked to help another inmate. He refused to do so and received threats against his family.

In XXX 2007, the claimant's brother was charged with theft: he was arrested and detained for over 24 hours. The claimant's father defended him, and the police officer told him that all the members of the family would serve prison time.

The claimant's brother was arrested again in XXXXX 2008. That same month, some police officers also stopped the claimant on a highway in the state of Mexico. The police officers told him that they would not arrest him immediately, but that he would soon be joining his brother in prison.

The claimant alleged that, from XXXX 2007 to XXXXX 2008, he was robbed four times. He also alleged that, in late XXXXX, he was robbed and beaten one street away from his home. Once more, on that occasion, he was threatened with joining his father in prison.

On that day, he filed a report with a police patrol. The patrol told him not to try anything against his assailants because the beatings were not visible. They also told him that, if he went to the station, it would be worse for him.

He decided to leave Mexico and arrived in Montréal on XXXXX, 2009. In XXXXX 2009, he found out that, when his brother was released in XXXXX 2009, he was beaten by people who were asking him for the claimant's whereabouts. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant's identity was established to the panel's satisfaction by means of his passport, which was seized by Immigration Canada. ANALYSIS Credibility
The claimant testified that he fears imprisonment because his father and brother were allegedly detained for tax evasion and for theft, respectively.

The claimant testified that, on his release from prison, his father, a XXXXX, received a letter from an inmate, asking him to defend him. After his father refused, the whole family allegedly received threats.
The claimant testified that his brother's arrest was precipitated by his father's refusal and that, should he return to Mexico, he would be next.

The claimant submitted as Exhibit M-1 a document from the Superior Court of Justice of the Federal District?Mexico, according to which the claimant's brother, XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, [translation] "is criminally responsible for committing the offence of attempted aggravated theft, which imposes a sentence of 10 (ten) months' imprisonment and twenty days of fines amounting to 1,011.40 pesos."1

That document corroborates the claimant's allegations that his brother was convicted of theft. However, the claimant did not establish that there is any connection between his brother's arrest and the fact that his father had refused to help an inmate prepare his defence.

When the panel asked the claimant at the hearing why the inmate seeking his father's help to be released had the power to have his brother arrested and convicted but was unable to manage his own release, the claimant gave no explanation.
The panel is surprised that inmates with power and influence would not have the means to find a lawyer to defend them.

The claimant also testified that, in XXXXX 2008, he was arrested on the highway to XXXXXX, in the state of Mexico, by police officers who told him that [translation] "soon he will be with his brother on the inside." When asked to explain how it is that police officers he met by chance on a highway far from his home were aware of his family's problems, the claimant explained that one of these police officers was present when his brother had been arrested the first time.
The panel is of the opinion that this is an adjustment of the testimony and does not believe that the claimant was threatened with joining his brother in prison.

Moreover, if this had been the case and the police officers had wanted to arrest him, why would they have not done it then? To this question, the claimant responded, at question 31 of his story, that the police officers allegedly told him: [translation] "... it's only a matter of time, because I was with my lover. But once I would be all alone, it would be different."2

The only corroborated allegation made by the claimant was his brother's arrest. He did not establish that his father was a XXXXX or that his father had had problems with respect to the contact that he had in prison.

The claimant arrived in Canada in XXXXX 2009. When asked why he waited until April 2010 to claim refugee protection, he answered [translation]: "I was waiting for the situation to improve." The panel notes that this explanation is not valid in that the claimant alleged that he is being followed by security officers and police officers who want to put him in prison; in such circumstances, it would be difficult to determine at what point the situation would improve.
The panel is of the opinion that this lengthy delay in claiming refugee protection is not consistent with the attitude of someone who fears for his life, and it undermines the claimant's credibility.
The panel finds this story not credible.

Having analyzed the testimonial and documentary evidence, the panel determines that the claimant failed to discharge his burden of establishing that there is a "serious possibility" that he would be persecuted on a Convention ground. He failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment, should he return to Mexico.
For all these reasons, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection.|"

The panel rejects the claim for refugee protection filed by XXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXX.
